items.title: Clocks — angle formula and hand-position events
items.body:
## Angle between the hands

- **Angle = |30H − 5.5M|** degrees (H = hour, M = minutes). If the result exceeds 180°, subtract from 360°.
- The minute hand moves **6°/min**, the hour hand **0.5°/min**, so the minute hand gains **5.5°/min** on the hour hand.

## When the hands meet / oppose / square up

| Event | Condition | In 12 hours | In 24 hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coincide (0°) | 30H = 5.5M | 11 | 22 |
| Opposite (180°) | \|30H − 5.5M\| = 180 | 11 | 22 |
| Right angle (90°) | \|30H − 5.5M\| = 90 | 22 | 44 |

## Worked example

At 3:40, angle = |30×3 − 5.5×40| = |90 − 220| = **130°**. Hands coincide every **720/11 = 65 5/11 min**; the overlap past hour H is at **60H/11** minutes.

## Trap

- Between 5 and 7 o'clock the hands are opposite only ONCE, which is why the 12-hour count is 11, not 12.
keyPoints: Angle between hands = |30H − 5.5M| degrees; take the value ≤ 180°.
Minute hand gains 5.5° per minute on the hour hand.
In 12 hours: coincide 11 times, opposite 11 times, right angles 22 times (double for 24 h).
Hands coincide every 65 5/11 minutes; overlap past hour H is at 60H/11 minutes.
Right-angle / opposite times solve |30H − 5.5M| = 90 or 180.
items.mnemonic: Remember '30H minus five-and-a-half M' — the 5.5 is the minute hand's per-minute gain.
items.source: local APPSC Logical Reasoning PDF — Clock

items.title: Clocks — faulty clocks and mirror images
items.body:
## Faulty (gaining / losing) clock

- **Total error = per-hour error × hours elapsed.**
- A **losing** clock shows an EARLIER time; a **gaining** clock shows a LATER time.
- Example: loses 3 min/hour, set right at 6 a.m. → in 24 h it loses 72 min = 1 h 12 min → shows **4:48 a.m.**
- 'Correct-time' problems: if a clock gains g and loses l over a span, find when the net error returns to zero.

## Mirror image

- **Mirror time = 12:00 − actual time** (use **11:60 − time** when minutes ≠ 00).
- Example: 3:25 → 11:60 − 3:25 = **8:35**.

## Water image

- Reference is **18:00 (6:00)**, not 12:00 — subtract the time from 18:30/etc. (a different reflection axis).

## Trap

- Don't confuse mirror (left–right, base 12:00) with water image (up–down, base 6:00).
keyPoints: Faulty-clock error = per-hour gain/loss × number of hours elapsed.
A losing clock reads earlier; a gaining clock reads later than true time.
Mirror image of a time = 12:00 − time (use 11:60 − time when minutes are non-zero).
Mirror example: 3:25 → 8:35.
Water image uses the 6:00 reference, distinct from the mirror's 12:00 reference.
items.source: local APPSC Logical Reasoning PDF — Clock

items.title: Calendars — odd days and finding the day of the week
items.body:
## Odd days

- **Odd days** = the days left over after removing complete weeks.
- 1 ordinary year = **1 odd day**; 1 leap year = **2 odd days**.
- Century totals: **100 yrs = 5, 200 yrs = 3, 300 yrs = 1, 400 yrs = 0** odd days.

## Month odd-days (ordinary year)

| Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 0 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 |

(In a leap year February contributes 1 odd day.)

## Finding the day

1. Add odd days from complete centuries + remaining years (count leap years as 2) + month odd-days + date.
2. Take the total **mod 7**; map **0 → Sunday, 1 → Monday, … 6 → Saturday**.

## Worked example

15 Aug 1947 → total odd days ≡ 5 ⇒ **Friday** (verified with datetime).
keyPoints: Odd days = remainder after removing whole weeks; ordinary year = 1, leap year = 2.
Map the total odd days mod 7: 0 = Sunday … 6 = Saturday.
Month odd-days (ordinary): 3,0,3,2,3,2,3,3,2,3,2,3.
15 August 1947 was a Friday.
items.mnemonic: Century odd-days count DOWN in twos: 5, 3, 1, 0.
items.source: local APPSC Logical Reasoning PDF — Calendar

items.title: Calendars — leap-year rule and calendar repetition
items.body:
## Leap-year rule

- A year is a leap year if **divisible by 4**, EXCEPT century years, which must be **divisible by 400**.
- So 2000 is a leap year; 1900 and 2100 are NOT.
- Leap year = 366 days (Feb 29); ordinary year = 365 days.

## Same date, next year

- The same date moves forward **1 day** after an ordinary year and **2 days** after a leap year.
- Example: 1 Jan 2024 (Mon) → 1 Jan 2025 is **Wednesday**, because 2024 is a leap year (+2).

## Calendar repetition

- A calendar repeats when the total odd days since that year ≡ **0 (mod 7)** AND leap-year status matches.
- **Ordinary years** typically repeat after **6 or 11 years**; **leap years** after **28 years**.
- Example: 2023's calendar repeats in **2034** (verified with datetime).
keyPoints: Leap year: divisible by 4, but century years must be divisible by 400.
2000 is a leap year; 1900 and 2100 are not.
Same date advances 1 day after an ordinary year, 2 days after a leap year.
A calendar repeats when odd days ≡ 0 mod 7 and leap-status matches.
Ordinary years repeat after 6/11 years; leap years after 28; 2023 repeats in 2034.
items.source: local APPSC Logical Reasoning PDF — Calendar

items.title: Ages — ratio, difference and average methods
items.body:
## Set-up

- **Ratio ages** → write parts as kx (e.g. 5x, 7x); add/subtract the SAME time to each, then equate to the new ratio and solve.
- **Difference** stays constant over time: if one is k years older, use A = B + k.
- **'N years ago'** → subtract N from BOTH ages before applying the relation; **'N years hence'** → add N to both.

## Averages of ages

- New member's age = new_avg × (n+1) − old_avg × n.
- **Shortcut:** added age = new average + (rise in average × number of old members).
- Example: 11 players avg 29; adding a coach raises avg to 30 → coach = 30 + 1×11 = **41**.

## Worked example

Ages 5x : 7x; six years hence 3:4 → 4(5x+6) = 3(7x+6) → x = 6 → **30 and 42 years**.

## Common traps

- Add the time to BOTH people, not just one.
- Ratios are NOT preserved as years pass — always re-solve.
keyPoints: Ratio ages: use parts kx, add the same time to each, equate to the new ratio, solve.
Age difference is constant; if one is k years older, A = B + k.
'N years ago' subtracts N from both ages; 'N years hence' adds N to both.
Added member's age = new_avg×(n+1) − old_avg×n; shortcut = new_avg + rise×(old count).
Ratios change over time, so re-solve rather than reusing the old ratio.
items.mnemonic: Ages move together — whatever you do to one age, do to the other.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Problem on Age / Based on Cricket and Age

items.title: Last day of a century & date-shift within a month
items.body:
**Last day of a century** follows a fixed 400-year cycle. The odd days for 100/200/300/400 years are 5/3/1/0, so the last day (31 Dec of a year ending in 00) can only be Friday, Wednesday, Monday or Sunday — it can **never be Tuesday, Thursday or Saturday**. (The same three days are also impossible as the *first* day of a century.)

**Date-shift within one month:** any two dates in the same month differ by a whole number of days, so the weekday advances by (difference mod 7).

*Example:* if the 5th is a Tuesday, the 21st is 21 − 5 = 16 days later; 16 mod 7 = 2, so the day is Tuesday + 2 = **Thursday**. Dates exactly 7, 14, 21 … apart fall on the same weekday.

**Trap:** count the GAP between the dates (16), not the date number itself, before taking mod 7.
keyPoints: Last day of a century is only Fri/Wed/Mon/Sun — never Tue/Thu/Sat
Within a month, weekday advances by (date difference mod 7)
5th = Tuesday ⇒ 21st = Tue + (16 mod 7 = 2) = Thursday
Dates 7/14/21 apart share the same weekday
items.source: Testbook Calendar Reasoning PYQ patterns; APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF
